gloss_terse: wall, fortification; defensive structure of a city, particularly bulwarks or buttresses
gloss_readable: This rare architectural term appears only in descriptions of Babylon's fortifications. The Hebrew preserves two variant readings (Ketiv/Qere) both pointing to defensive structures—either the foundational bulwarks or the supporting buttresses that reinforced city walls. The term is a loan-word from Aramaic, related to words meaning 'column' or 'support' across several ancient Near Eastern languages.

senses.1: Both occurrences in Jeremiah 50:15 refer to Babylon's defensive architecture, used in parallel with 'her walls' (חוֹמוֹתֶיהָ). The multilingual evidence shows translators struggling with this rare term—some rendering it as 'foundations' (English, Spanish 'cimientos'), others preserving the transliteration. The Aramaic cognates and Talmudic usage confirm this refers to structural supports, whether foundational bulwarks or vertical buttresses that gave strength to fortification walls.

gloss_terse: Ashchur; personal name, 'father of Tekoa' in Judah's genealogy
gloss_readable: A personal name appearing in the genealogies of Judah, specifically identified as 'the father of Tekoa.' The exact meaning of the name remains uncertain, though it appears in the intricate genealogical records of 1 Chronicles. Ancient translations render it variously, reflecting the difficulty of determining whether this represents an individual or a clan designation.

senses.1: This name appears twice in Chronicles' genealogies (1 Chr 2:24; 4:5), both times with the designation 'father of Tekoa'—likely indicating either the founder or a prominent leader of that Judahite town. The Greek translations vary significantly (Ασχω, Σαρα, Ασδωδ, Ασχουρ), suggesting ancient translators also found this name challenging. The phrase 'father of' in genealogical contexts often denotes city founders or clan heads rather than literal paternity.

gloss_terse: gift, tribute; payment or present given as honor
gloss_readable: This term denotes a gift or tribute given to honor a superior, appearing in poetic contexts describing royal protocol. It occurs alongside the more common word for offering (מִנְחָה), suggesting formal gifts presented to kings or rulers. The rare word carries connotations of payment or compensation in contexts of international diplomacy or trade.

senses.1: The two occurrences illustrate different contexts of gift-giving: Psalm 72:10 depicts kings bringing tribute ('gifts') to Israel's monarch in parallel with 'offerings' (מִנְחָה), while Ezekiel 27:15 describes commercial 'payment' given to Tyre for trade goods. The multilingual glosses consistently render this as 'gift' (English, German), 'present/tribute' (Spanish 'presente/tributo'), or 'cadeau' (French), all emphasizing the honorific or compensatory nature of the transaction rather than voluntary generosity.

gloss_terse: lattice, window-lattice; wooden or stone screen covering a window opening
gloss_readable: This architectural term describes the latticed screen or framework that covered window openings in ancient buildings. Used in parallel with 'window' (חַלּוֹן), it refers to the decorative or protective grillwork that allowed air and light while providing privacy and security. Both biblical occurrences picture women looking through these lattices—one anxiously, one seductively.

senses.1: The lattice appears in two memorable scenes: Sisera's mother peering anxiously through the window-lattice awaiting her son's return (Judges 5:28), and the 'strange woman' looking through her lattice to entice the simple youth (Proverbs 7:6). The architectural element suggests upper-story windows in substantial houses. Translations consistently render this as 'lattice' or 'celosía' (Spanish), capturing the screened nature of the opening. The Hebrew term likely derives from a root related to Ben Sira's usage, suggesting well-established architectural vocabulary.

gloss_terse: Ashnah; name of two cities in Judah
gloss_readable: A place name appearing in the territorial allotments of Judah, designating two distinct cities. The name may derive from a root meaning 'firm' or 'strong,' though this etymology remains uncertain. Both cities were located in the Shephelah, the lowland region of Judah.

senses.1: Joshua 15 lists two separate cities named Ashnah in Judah's inheritance: one in verse 33 (in the lowland district), another in verse 43 (in a different lowland section). The consistent multilingual rendering simply transliterates the name (Asná, Ashnah), treating it as a proper geographical designation. The duplication of the name within the same tribal territory likely reflects distinct settlements, perhaps named for similar topographical features or founding circumstances.

gloss_terse: enchanter, conjurer; practitioner of incantations and magic
gloss_readable: A term for Babylonian magicians or sorcerers, likely borrowed from Akkadian (âšipu), referring to specialists in incantations and divination. The word appears only in Daniel's court narratives, grouped with other classes of Babylonian wise men. These were professional practitioners of magical arts, distinct from but associated with astrologers and diviners.

senses.1: Both occurrences in Daniel (1:20; 2:2) list enchanters alongside other categories of Babylonian court specialists—magicians (חַרְטֻמִּים), sorcerers (מְכַשְּׁפִים), and Chaldeans (כַּשְׂדִּים). Daniel 1:20 notes that Daniel and his friends were 'ten times better' than all these practitioners. The Babylonian loan-word reflects the specialized vocabulary of Mesopotamian magical professions, and the Aramaic cognates confirm this denotes ritual specialists who performed conjurations. Translations render it as 'enchanters' (English), 'encantadores' (Spanish), or preserve the transliteration, recognizing the technical nature of this professional class.

gloss_terse: date-cake, portion; food item distributed at celebration, possibly pressed dates or meat
gloss_readable: A food item distributed to the people during David's celebration when the ark was brought to Jerusalem. The exact nature of this portion remains uncertain—ancient and modern interpreters have variously suggested date cakes, raisin cakes, or portions of meat. The word appears only in the parallel accounts of this single festive occasion.

senses.1: At the ark's arrival in Jerusalem, David distributed to all Israel 'a loaf of bread, a portion of meat, and a cake' (2 Samuel 6:19 = 1 Chronicles 16:3). This middle item's identity puzzled even ancient translators: the Greek Septuagint suggested 'cake or roll,' while modern versions waver between 'date cake' and 'portion of meat.' The uncertainty appears in multilingual glosses, where some transliterations simply preserve the Hebrew. The festive context suggests a choice food item, and the parallel structure indicates three distinct elements of the celebratory distribution.

gloss_terse: relative pronoun; 'who,' 'which,' 'that,' marking relative clauses
gloss_readable: The primary relative pronoun in Biblical Hebrew, functioning to introduce relative clauses and link descriptive information to nouns. This grammatical particle appears thousands of times throughout the Hebrew Bible, serving as one of the most common function words in the language. Its usage here represents variant spellings or textual readings.

senses.1: These two occurrences (2 Samuel 23:21; Ezekiel 9:11) represent the standard relative pronoun function, likely marked in the data due to variant spellings or Ketiv/Qere readings. The multilingual evidence shows this functioning as 'that/which/who' (que, qui, welcher), confirming its role as a relativizer linking clauses. The particle is so fundamental to Hebrew syntax that it serves as the standard way to create relative clauses, analogous to 'that/which/who' in English.

gloss_terse: step, footstep; the act of walking or one's course of movement
gloss_readable: A poetic term for steps or footsteps, used metaphorically for one's path or conduct in life. The word appears in wisdom and prayer contexts, where physical walking serves as an image for moral behavior and life direction. Both occurrences use possessive suffixes, personalizing the imagery of one's journey.

senses.1: Job protests his integrity by asking if his 'step has turned from the way' (Job 31:7), using walking as a metaphor for moral conduct. The Psalmist prays concerning 'our steps' being tracked by enemies (Psalm 17:11). The imagery of steps/walking for life-conduct is common in Hebrew poetry. The multilingual evidence shows interesting variation: while English and Spanish render it literally as 'step/paso,' French substitutes 'bonheur' (happiness) in Job, possibly reading a different root, and German follows with 'gluecklich' (happy/blessed), perhaps influenced by the similar-sounding אַשְׁרֵי (blessed).

gloss_terse: wall, structure; building component, possibly wall or sanctuary element
gloss_readable: An Aramaic architectural term appearing in Ezra's account of the temple rebuilding, used alongside 'house' to describe construction work. The exact meaning remains debated—most suggest 'wall,' though some scholars propose 'sanctuary' based on Akkadian cognates. The Persian-era context and parallel with 'house' suggest a major structural element of the temple reconstruction.

senses.1: In Ezra 5, Persian officials question the Jews: 'Who gave you permission to build this house and complete this structure?' (vv. 3, 9). The term pairs with 'house' (בַּיְתָא), suggesting either walls as distinct from the building proper, or perhaps the temple's sacred inner structures. Translations vary: most render 'wall' (Spanish 'muro'), while others transliterate, acknowledging uncertainty. The Masoretic pointing suggests a connection to earlier Hebrew אֻשַּׁיָּא, but the exact architectural referent remains elusive. The Aramaic context and Akkadian parallels point to substantial structural elements of the Second Temple construction.

gloss_terse: sedition, revolt; rebellious uprising against authority
gloss_readable: An Aramaic term for political rebellion or sedition, used in the hostile letters sent to Persian authorities accusing Jerusalem of having a history of revolt. The word appears in Persian-period correspondence attempting to halt the rebuilding of Jerusalem by portraying the city as a persistent threat to imperial stability.

senses.1: The accusers write to King Artaxerxes claiming that investigation of historical records will reveal 'rebellion and sedition' have been carried out in Jerusalem (Ezra 4:15, 19). The term is part of a threefold accusation—'rebellion, sedition, and insurrection'—designed to alarm Persian authorities about Jerusalem's restoration. This Aramaic vocabulary of political resistance appears in official correspondence, reflecting the administrative language of the Persian Empire. The multilingual glosses render it as 'sedition' (English/Spanish 'sedición') or preserve the transliteration, recognizing its technical administrative-legal meaning.

gloss_terse: Eshton; personal name in Judah's genealogy
gloss_readable: A personal name in the genealogies of Judah, appearing in the lineage of Chelub. The etymology may relate to a root meaning 'effeminate' or 'uxorious' (devoted to one's wife), though this remains speculative. The name appears only in the detailed genealogical records preserved in 1 Chronicles.

senses.1: Eshton appears twice in rapid succession in 1 Chronicles 4:11-12 as part of Judah's descendant list, identified as related to Chelub and as the father of Beth-rapha, Paseah, and Tehinnah. Ancient translations simply transliterate the name (Eston, Eshton), treating it as an opaque personal designation. The genealogical context provides no additional information about this individual beyond his placement in Judah's family tree, and the suggested etymology from אֵשֶׁת (wife) remains uncertain.

gloss_terse: Beer; place name meaning 'well'
gloss_readable: A geographical name meaning simply 'well,' designating locations marked by water sources. The common noun for well (בְּאֵר) became a place name at multiple sites in ancient Israel, understandably given the vital importance of water sources in the arid climate. Both biblical occurrences mark significant locations in Israel's wilderness journeys and early settlement.

senses.1: Two distinct locations bear this name: one where Israel stopped and sang the well-song during wilderness wanderings (Numbers 21:16), and another where Jotham fled after pronouncing his parable against Abimelech (Judges 9:21). The transparent meaning 'well' made this a natural place name, and multilingual glosses simply transliterate it as a proper name (Beer). The Numbers passage includes the famous song, 'Spring up, O well!' suggesting this Beer was particularly associated with water discovery. Multiple sites may have shared this descriptive name, much like modern towns named 'Springs' or 'Wells.'

gloss_terse: Beeri; personal name meaning 'my well'
gloss_readable: A personal name meaning 'my well,' borne by two individuals in Scripture: a Hittite who became Esau's father-in-law, and Hosea's father. The possessive form suggests either a theophoric meaning (Yahweh as 'my well/source') or simply a name derived from association with a well.

senses.1: Two men bear this name: first, Beeri the Hittite, whose daughter Judith married Esau, causing 'grief of mind' to Isaac and Rebekah (Genesis 26:34); second, Beeri the father of the prophet Hosea (Hosea 1:1). The name's meaning 'my well' could reflect gratitude for water sources or, more likely, metaphorical use where God is viewed as one's source or well of life. The multilingual glosses simply transliterate (Beeri, Bééri), treating it as an opaque proper name. Notably, one Beeri was Hittite (non-Israelite), while the other fathered a major prophet, showing the name crossed ethnic boundaries.

gloss_terse: wild grapes, worthless grapes; sour or inedible fruit from untended vines
gloss_readable: A term describing the inferior, worthless fruit produced by a vineyard despite careful cultivation. Isaiah uses this in his allegory of Yahweh's vineyard, where despite every advantage, Israel produced wild or stinking grapes instead of good fruit. The word emphasizes the corrupt or worthless nature of what grew, perhaps stinking or sour grapes in contrast to cultivated varieties.

senses.1: Both occurrences appear in Isaiah's vineyard song (5:2, 4), where God planted a choice vineyard with every advantage but 'it yielded wild grapes' instead of good fruit. The Hebrew may derive from a root meaning 'stink' or 'be worthless,' suggesting grapes that are rotten, sour, or otherwise inedible. Translations consistently render this as 'wild grapes' (English, Spanish 'uvas silvestres'), distinguishing cultivated from wild varieties. The allegory makes Israel's moral failure vivid: despite divine care, they produced corrupt fruit—injustice instead of justice, outcry instead of righteousness. The term captures both the unexpectedness and the worthlessness of what resulted.

gloss_terse: treachery, faithlessness; betrayal or breach of trust
gloss_readable: A term denoting treachery or faithless dealing, derived from the root meaning 'to act treacherously.' This abstract noun appears in prophetic oracles condemning breach of covenant or betrayal of trust. The word emphasizes the violation of relationship rather than merely breaking rules—unfaithfulness to persons or commitments.

senses.1: Isaiah laments, 'Treachery, treachery! The treacherous deal very treacherously!' (24:16), using wordplay to intensify the indictment. Jeremiah asks God why the treacherous prosper (12:1), using the noun alongside related verbal forms. The multilingual evidence shows confusion: some translations render 'treachery/traición' (English, Spanish), while others give 'vêtement' (French, German following differently), suggesting they read this as the homonym בֶּגֶד (garment) instead. This confusion in translation history highlights how context must distinguish between identical spellings denoting either 'garment' or 'treachery.' The prophetic contexts clearly demand the meaning 'treachery'—covenant unfaithfulness personified.

gloss_terse: treacherous (feminine adjective); characterized by unfaithfulness or betrayal
gloss_readable: The feminine adjectival form describing someone or something characterized by treachery. Jeremiah uses this exclusively for personified Judah and her sister Israel, depicting the nation as an unfaithful woman who betrays her covenant relationship with Yahweh. The adjective carries strong relational overtones of infidelity and broken trust.

senses.1: Jeremiah addresses 'treacherous Judah' and 'faithless Israel' using feminine forms (3:7, 10), employing the metaphor of unfaithful sisters to describe the two kingdoms' covenant violations. The adjective appears in God's commentary on whether Judah had truly returned with her whole heart or only in pretense. The feminine form matches the personification of nations as women in prophetic marriage metaphors. Multilingual glosses render this as 'the treacherous one' (English, Spanish 'la traidora'), preserving the feminine gender that reinforces the marriage imagery. The word choice intensifies the personal dimension of covenant breaking—not mere law violation but marital betrayal.

gloss_terse: Bigthan/Bigthana; personal name of a Persian court official
gloss_readable: The name of a eunuch serving in King Ahasuerus's court who, along with Teresh, conspired to assassinate the Persian king. The name appears to be Persian in origin, possibly meaning 'gift of God.' The plot was discovered by Mordecai, an event that later proved crucial to the deliverance of the Jews. The name appears in two variant spellings.

senses.1: Bigthan (also Bigthana) was one of two royal chamberlains who 'sought to lay hands on King Ahasuerus' (Esther 2:21; 6:2). Mordecai discovered and reported the conspiracy, which was investigated and the conspirators executed. The later reading of these records before the sleepless king led to Mordecai's honor and Haman's downfall. The variant spellings (בִּגְתָן/בִּגְתָנָא) likely represent the same individual, with the second form showing Aramaic influence. Persian royal courts employed eunuchs as chamberlains, and the name reflects Persian naming patterns with possible theophoric elements (bagadâna, 'gift of God').

gloss_terse: devise, invent; fabricate or originate (in negative sense)
gloss_readable: A verb meaning to devise, invent, or fabricate, used exclusively in negative contexts for contriving falsehoods or unauthorized innovations. The word appears in accusations of invention—whether inventing false charges or devising unauthorized religious practices. Both occurrences highlight fabrication without proper authority or truth.

senses.1: Jeroboam 'devised' a feast on a date 'of his own heart'—an unauthorized religious innovation (1 Kings 12:33). Nehemiah accuses his opponents: 'You are inventing them out of your own heart'—fabricating false charges (Nehemiah 6:8). The verb consistently carries negative connotations of fabrication without warrant. Multilingual glosses render this as 'devise/invent' (English, Spanish 'inventó/inventas'), capturing the sense of origination that is unauthorized or false. The Mishnaic Hebrew and Aramaic cognates maintain this meaning of invention. Both contexts involve either religious innovation without divine sanction or political accusation without factual basis—fabrication in realms where truth and authority matter most.

gloss_terse: Bedad; personal name, father of an Edomite ruler
gloss_readable: A personal name appearing in the genealogical lists of Edomite kings, identified as the father of Hadad who defeated Midian. The name appears in the formulaic 'son of Bedad' construction typical of ancient king lists. Its etymology remains uncertain.

senses.1: Bedad is known solely as the father of Hadad, the Edomite king 'who defeated Midian in the country of Moab' (Genesis 36:35 = 1 Chronicles 1:46). The parallel genealogies preserve identical information, listing him in the early Edomite royal succession before Israel had kings. The name is simply transliterated across translations (Bedad, Bedads), treated as an opaque proper designation. The formulaic 'Hadad son of Bedad' follows standard ancient Near Eastern patterns for identifying rulers by patronymic. No other information about Bedad survives beyond his identity as father of this victorious king.

gloss_terse: bdellium; aromatic gum resin, yellowish and transparent
gloss_readable: An aromatic gum resin, likely yellowish and transparent, used in two quite different comparisons in Scripture. Genesis lists it among the valuable products of the land of Havilah, while Numbers compares its appearance to manna. Ancient and modern interpreters have debated whether this refers to a fragrant gum (the majority view) or to pearls, given divergent ancient translations.

senses.1: Genesis 2:12 lists bdellium alongside gold and onyx as products of Havilah, suggesting a valuable commodity. Numbers 11:7 describes manna's appearance: 'its color was like the color of bdellium'—apparently a comparison of visual appearance, suggesting something translucent and yellowish. The multilingual evidence shows ancient uncertainty: the Greek Septuagint gave 'carbuncle' in Genesis but 'crystal' in Numbers; most moderns follow the Latin 'bdellium,' identifying an aromatic transparent gum. The definite article ('the bdellium') suggests a well-known substance. Josephus and later versions support the gum identification—an odoriferous, yellowish, transparent resin collected from trees. The comparison to manna's color favors something translucent rather than opaque pearls.

gloss_terse: Bedan; personal name of uncertain identification
gloss_readable: A personal name appearing in two unrelated contexts: once in Samuel's list of judges (though textual uncertainty exists) and once in Manassite genealogy. The first occurrence is textually problematic, with many scholars suggesting it represents a corruption of 'Barak.' The etymology may relate to a name meaning 'servant,' though this remains speculative.

senses.1: In 1 Samuel 12:11, Samuel lists deliverers including 'Bedan,' but this name appears nowhere else in Judges' narratives. The Septuagint and Syriac read 'Barak' instead, widely accepted as the original reading (cf. Judges 4-5). A different Bedan appears as a Manassite in genealogy (1 Chronicles 7:17). The multilingual glosses simply transliterate (Bedan, Bedán), treating it as a proper name. The textual problem in Samuel makes the first reference uncertain—possibly a scribal error for Barak, or perhaps a judge otherwise unrecorded. The Chronicles occurrence stands without this difficulty, representing a legitimate Manassite name, possibly a shortened form of Abdan (servant).

gloss_terse: Bohan; personal name used to designate a boundary stone
gloss_readable: A personal name meaning possibly 'thumb' or 'closing/covering,' preserved in the designation of a boundary marker between Judah and Benjamin: 'the stone of Bohan son of Reuben.' This stone served as a recognizable landmark in territorial descriptions. The name's etymology remains debated.

senses.1: The 'stone of Bohan son of Reuben' marked the boundary between Judah and Benjamin (Joshua 15:6; 18:17). The designation preserves the name of a Reubenite, though nothing else is known of this individual. Whether Bohan erected the stone or it was named after him for other reasons is unclear. The name may relate to בֹּהֶן (thumb), suggesting physical characteristics or symbolic meaning. Multilingual glosses simply transliterate (Bohan, Boján), treating it as an opaque proper name. The patronymic 'son of Reuben' is unusual in geographical designations, perhaps indicating this Bohan was a notable early settler or boundary commissioner from the tribe of Reuben, or that the stone itself resembled a thumb.

gloss_terse: Buzite; gentilic indicating descent from Buz
gloss_readable: An ethnic or family designation meaning 'descended from Buz,' used exclusively for Elihu's father Barachel in the book of Job. The Buzites traced their ancestry to Buz, Abraham's nephew (Genesis 22:21), placing them among Aramean peoples related to Israel. The designation appears with the definite article, 'the Buzite,' marking it as a known ethnic group.

senses.1: Elihu is introduced as 'Barachel the Buzite' (Job 32:2, 6), identifying his family origin among the descendants of Buz, son of Nahor and Milcah (Genesis 22:21). This places Elihu's lineage among the Aramean peoples of northern Mesopotamia, related to but distinct from Israelites. The definite article in both occurrences ('the Buzite') indicates a recognized ethnic designation. Buz is also mentioned alongside Dedan as an Arabian people in Jeremiah 25:23, suggesting the Buzites inhabited regions between Aram and Arabia. The careful ethnic identification in Job distinguishes Elihu from Job's three friends, who came from other related but distinct peoples (Temanite, Shuhite, Naamathite).

gloss_terse: product, growth; what grows from or is produced by something
gloss_readable: A term denoting the product or outgrowth of something, used for what mountains produce or what comes from a tree. The word emphasizes origin—what grows from or is yielded by a source. Both biblical uses focus on natural production, whether agricultural or simply the wood that comes from a tree.

senses.1: Job 40:20 describes behemoth with 'the mountains yield produce for him'—the vegetation that grows on hills provides his food. Isaiah 44:19 speaks of a block of wood as 'the product of a tree' (literally 'tree-growth') that someone then carves into an idol. The term emphasizes source and derivation: what the mountains grow, what comes from a tree. Some suggest this is an abbreviated form of יְבוּל (produce), or possibly a scribal variant. Multilingual glosses vary—some render 'product/produce,' others transliterate, reflecting uncertainty about this rare term. The contexts clearly indicate natural yield or growth—agricultural produce in Job, raw wood material in Isaiah.

gloss_terse: divide, cut through; split or cleave (of rivers dividing land)
gloss_readable: A verb meaning to divide or cut through, used specifically of rivers dividing or traversing a land. The word appears only in Isaiah's oracles concerning Cush, describing how rivers cut through that territory. The term likely relates to Aramaic roots meaning 'cleave' or 'split.'

senses.1: Both occurrences describe Cush as 'a land whose rivers divide it' or 'cut through it' (Isaiah 18:2, 7). The image depicts the geography of Cush (likely ancient Nubia/Ethiopia), characterized by rivers that traverse and partition the territory—probably the Nile and its tributaries cutting through the land. The Hebrew may relate to Aramaic בְּזַע (cleave), suggesting rivers that split or section the terrain. Multilingual translations show uncertainty: some render 'divided/despojado' (divided/despoiled), others transliterate. The geographical context strongly supports the meaning of rivers cutting through or dividing the land, creating a territory characterized by watercourses that section it into distinct regions.

gloss_terse: scatter, disperse; distribute by scattering
gloss_readable: A verb meaning to scatter or disperse, used of distributing plunder among followers or dispersing peoples. Related to Arabic and Aramaic roots for scattering seed or dispersing, the term emphasizes distribution through spreading out. Both occurrences involve deliberate scattering—either of spoils or of peoples.

senses.1: The Psalm calls on God to 'scatter the peoples who delight in war' (68:30), asking for the dispersal of warlike nations. Daniel prophesies that the king of the north 'will scatter among them plunder, spoil, and possessions' (11:24)—Antiochus Epiphanes distributing conquered goods to his followers. The verb emphasizes distribution through scattering: whether dispersing peoples or spreading out spoils among supporters. Multilingual glosses render 'scatter/dispersa/disperser' (scatter/disperse), with French also offering 'diviser' (divide). The Arabic cognate بَذَرَ (scatter seed) and Aramaic בְּדַר (scatter) support this meaning of distribution through dispersal. Both contexts involve deliberate strategic scattering—either of military opponents or material rewards.

gloss_terse: fortresses, citadels; fortified strongholds
gloss_readable: A late Hebrew term for fortresses or fortified places, appearing only in Chronicles' accounts of Jehoshaphat's and Jotham's building projects. The plural noun denotes substantial military installations—citadels or fortified strongholds built to secure the kingdom. The word pairs with 'storage cities' and 'towers,' indicating a category of defensive architecture.

senses.1: Jehoshaphat 'built fortresses and storage cities in Judah' (2 Chronicles 17:12), while Jotham 'built fortresses and towers in the hill country' (27:4). Both texts describe extensive royal building programs establishing military infrastructure throughout Judah's territory. The term represents late Biblical Hebrew vocabulary for permanent fortified installations, distinct from temporary field fortifications. Multilingual glosses render this as 'fortresses/fortalezas' or transliterate it. The Hebrew בִּירָנִיּוֹת appears to derive from בִּירָה (citadel, fortress), itself probably from Akkadian birtu. These were substantial defensive structures, part of the southern kingdom's military defensive network in the hill country and strategic locations.

gloss_terse: Beth-baal-meon; place name meaning 'house/temple of Baal-meon'
gloss_readable: A Transjordanian city name with several variant forms in Scripture, located in territory disputed between Reuben and Moab. The full form means 'house (or temple) of Baal-meon,' indicating a shrine to the deity Baal-meon. The site appears in various shortened forms across biblical texts, reflecting common practice of abbreviating compound place names.

senses.1: This city appears in multiple forms: Beth-baal-meon (Joshua 13:17), Baal-meon (Numbers 32:38; Ezekiel 25:9), Beth-meon (Jeremiah 48:23), and possibly Beon (Numbers 32:3). Assigned initially to Reuben, it later came under Moabite control, appearing in Jeremiah's oracle against Moab. The Moabite Stone also mentions it (as בעל מען and בת בעל מען), confirming its Moabite significance. Modern Ma'în preserves the name. The 'Beth' (house/temple) prefix indicates a cultic site, likely a sanctuary of the deity Baal-meon. The various abbreviated forms—dropping either 'Beth' or 'Baal' or both—illustrate how compound place names were flexibly shortened in usage.

gloss_terse: Beth-barah; place name, likely meaning 'house/place of the ford'
gloss_readable: A location mentioned in connection with the Jordan River and its waters during Gideon's pursuit of the Midianites. The name likely means 'place of the ford,' suggesting a strategic river crossing. The site is mentioned twice in rapid succession, indicating its significance as a control point for the fords of the Jordan.

senses.1: When Gideon pursued the Midianites, he called on Ephraimites to 'seize the waters as far as Beth-barah and the Jordan' (Judges 7:24, twice). The double mention emphasizes the strategic importance of controlling this crossing point. The name's suggested etymology—from עֲבָרָה (ford, crossing)—fits the military context perfectly: Beth-barah designated the ford-place where enemies could be intercepted as they attempted to cross the Jordan. The Ephraimites successfully seized these water crossings, cutting off the Midianite retreat. No other biblical references to this site survive, but its strategic position in Gideon's narrative clarifies its nature as a key Jordan River crossing in the central region.

gloss_terse: Beth-dagon; place name meaning 'house/temple of Dagon'
gloss_readable: A place name meaning 'temple of Dagon,' designating two distinct cities—one in Judah, one in Asher. The name indicates sites where the Philistine grain-deity Dagon was worshiped, likely Canaanite cult centers that predated Israelite settlement or reflected Philistine influence. Modern villages in both regions preserve forms of the name.

senses.1: Two cities bore this name: one in Judah's Shephelah (Joshua 15:41), another in Asher's territory (19:27). Both names indicate temples or cult sites of Dagon, the grain god prominent in Philistine religion (cf. 1 Samuel 5). Jerome defined it as 'house of wheat,' connecting Dagon to grain (דָּגָן), though the deity's fish associations (דָּג, fish) also appear in ancient sources. The Assyrian records mention Bît-Daganna in the region. Modern villages (Beit Dejân, Beit Dejen) preserve the name in both areas. These sites likely represent Canaanite cult centers absorbed into Israelite territory, their names honestly preserving the pre-Israelite religious history rather than being sanitized through renaming.

gloss_terse: Beth-haccherem; place name meaning 'house/place of the vineyard'
gloss_readable: A location in Judah whose name means 'vineyard place,' mentioned as both a signal point and an administrative district. The name reflects the agricultural character of the region, known for viticulture. The site's exact location remains debated, though it clearly held some strategic or administrative importance.

senses.1: Jeremiah calls for raising a signal 'in Beth-haccherem' as Babylon approaches (6:1), indicating a prominent or strategic location. Nehemiah identifies it as an administrative district with its own ruler who participated in rebuilding Jerusalem's walls (3:14). The name 'vineyard place' suggests agricultural prominence, appropriate for Judah's wine-growing regions. The location remains uncertain despite ancient discussion—some proposed sites near Tekoa, others between Jerusalem and coastal regions. The dual mention (prophetic signal-point and administrative district) confirms its significance in the Persian and late monarchic periods. The variant spellings (בֵּית הַכֶּרֶם/בֵּית הַכָּרֶם) represent the same location, with slight orthographic differences.

gloss_terse: at the far house; location marker, possibly 'Beth-merhak' (Far House)
gloss_readable: A phrase describing a location 'at the far house' or 'the distant place,' appearing when David fled Jerusalem during Absalom's revolt. Whether this represents a proper place name (Beth-merhak, 'Far House') or simply a descriptive phrase ('the last house of the city') remains debated. The context suggests a specific stopping point on the edge of Jerusalem.

senses.1: As David fled Jerusalem, he stopped 'at the far house' or 'at Beth-merhak' (2 Samuel 15:17, mentioned twice in the verse). The context shows this marked the city's edge—David stopped there while his servants passed before him. Some interpreters take this as a proper name: 'Far House,' a settlement or landmark at Jerusalem's outskirts. Others understand it descriptively: 'the last house' or 'the distant place,' marking where the city ended. The multilingual evidence divides: some render it as location ('at the house'), others emphasize distance ('the distant'). The Hebrew article suggests a known location, whether properly named 'Beth-merhak' or simply the recognized boundary point, the 'far house' beyond which lay open country.

gloss_terse: Beth-marcaboth; place name meaning 'house/place of chariots'
gloss_readable: A city in Simeon's territory whose name means 'place of chariots,' suggesting it served as a chariot base or storage facility. The name appears in variant spellings in the parallel tribal allotments, both clearly referring to the same location. The site's exact modern location remains unknown.

senses.1: This Simeonite city appears as 'Beth-marcaboth' (1 Chronicles 4:31) and 'Beth-ha-markaboth' (with the definite article, Joshua 19:5). The name 'chariot-place' suggests military significance—likely a garrison or storage facility for chariots, important military assets in ancient warfare. Simeon's cities were actually enclaves within Judah's larger territory (Joshua 19:1), so this chariot-city served defensive purposes for the southern tribes. The variant forms (with and without the definite article) represent normal variation in compound place names. Multilingual glosses transliterate the name, recognizing it as a proper geographical designation. No information about the site's specific location has survived, though it must have been significant enough to warrant designation as a chariot base.

gloss_terse: Beth-shemeshite; gentilic indicating a resident of Beth-shemesh
gloss_readable: An ethnic designation meaning 'inhabitant of Beth-shemesh,' used with the definite article to identify people from that Levitical city in Judah. The term appears in the narrative of the ark's return from Philistine territory, when it arrived at Beth-shemesh. The definite article indicates a recognized group—'the Beth-shemeshites.'

senses.1: When the ark came to Beth-shemesh from Philistia, the account mentions 'the Beth-shemeshite' or 'of the Beth-shemeshites' (1 Samuel 6:14, 18), referring to the people or property of that city. The definite article in both occurrences ('the Beth-shemeshite') indicates the recognized inhabitants of Beth-shemesh as a collective group. Beth-shemesh was a Levitical city on Judah's northern border, and its residents witnessed the ark's return and the divine judgment that followed. The gentilic formation (-ī ending) follows standard Hebrew patterns for ethnic/geographical designations. Multilingual glosses render this as 'the Beth-shemeshite' or 'el bet-shemesita,' preserving the ethnic designation and definite article that mark these people as the recognized community of that border city.

gloss_terse: Beth-maacah; place name, 'house/place of Maacah'
gloss_readable: A city in northern Israel, usually appearing in compound form as 'Abel of Beth-maacah.' The name indicates association with Maacah, possibly the small Aramean kingdom east of the Jordan, or a local clan/region. The site played a role in narratives of pursuit and invasion in the northern territories.

senses.1: The city appears most commonly as 'Abel Beth-maacah' (1 Kings 15:20; 2 Kings 15:29), but the shorter form 'Beth-maacah' occurs when Joab pursued Sheba there (2 Samuel 20:14-15). The name suggests connection to Maacah—either the Aramean kingdom (2 Samuel 10:6-8) or a regional designation. Located in Israel's far north, it faced Syrian invasions and Assyrian conquest. The account of the wise woman who saved the city (2 Samuel 20) reveals its significance as a 'mother city in Israel.' The variants with and without 'Abel' represent the same location, with Abel (meadow) perhaps describing its setting near water sources. The connection to Maacah (whether kingdom, clan, or region) remains uncertain, but the dual-component name indicates a settlement in or associated with Maacah territory.

gloss_terse: Beth-nimrah; place name meaning 'house of leopard/clear water'
gloss_readable: A Transjordanian city in Gad's territory whose name may mean either 'leopard place' or 'place of clear water.' The site lay east of the Jordan in the well-watered plains, and modern Tell Nimrîn preserves the name. The city appears in territorial allotments and is associated with nearby waters of Nimrim mentioned in prophetic oracles.

senses.1: Beth-nimrah was assigned to Gad in the Transjordanian allotments (Numbers 32:36; Joshua 13:27). The name likely derives from נָמֵר (leopard) or relates to the 'waters of Nimrim' (מֵי נִמְרִים) mentioned in Isaiah 15:6 and Jeremiah 48:34, suggesting association with springs or clear waters. Modern Tell Nimrîn, in the Jordan valley plains east of the river, preserves the ancient name. The well-watered location made it attractive for settlement, and its mention alongside 'cities of the valley' (Numbers 32:36) confirms its placement in the Jordan valley's eastern plain. Whether 'Nimrah' refers to leopards once inhabiting the area or to the character of its water sources (perhaps clear/pure), the name connected the city to its natural environment.

gloss_terse: first-ripe fig, early fig; prized early fruit of the fig tree
gloss_readable: The first-ripe or early fig, regarded as a delicacy and appearing before the main crop. These early figs ripened in late spring, ahead of the regular summer harvest, and were especially prized for their taste. Prophetic texts use the early fig as an image of something precious or eagerly desired.

senses.1: Hosea compares God's initial encounter with Israel to finding 'early figs on the fig tree in its first season' (9:10)—something delightful and unexpected. Micah laments his righteous state: there are no early figs to satisfy desire (7:1), using scarcity of this delicacy as metaphor for absence of godly people. Isaiah likewise uses 'first-ripe fig' for something eagerly devoured the moment it appears (28:4). The term (בִּכּוּרָה) relates to בִּכּוּרִים (firstfruits), emphasizing the early timing that made these figs valuable. Arabic (bākūrah) and Spanish (albacora) borrowings confirm the term's reference to early figs. These spring figs arrived before the main harvest, making them rare and eagerly anticipated—a perfect image for something precious and quickly consumed.

gloss_terse: Bochim; place name meaning 'weepers'
gloss_readable: A place name meaning 'weepers,' derived from an incident where Israel wept after divine rebuke. Located near Bethel, the site received its name when the people wept in response to the angel of the LORD's message about their covenant disobedience. Some scholars suggest connection with the oak of weeping (Allon-bacuth) near Bethel.

senses.1: The angel of the LORD came from Gilgal to 'Bochim' (the weepers) and rebuked Israel for covenant unfaithfulness (Judges 2:1, 5). After hearing this message, 'the people wept,' giving the place its name. The Greek varies between 'the weeping' (singular) and 'weepings' (plural), with some suggesting the reading 'Bethel' instead. Possible connection exists with Allon-bacuth ('oak of weeping') where Rebekah's nurse was buried near Bethel (Genesis 35:8), though this remains uncertain. The name commemorates a moment of national repentance—Israel's weeping response to divine rebuke about their failure to fully drive out the Canaanites and their compromises with local worship. The location near Bethel fits both the geography and the significance of this confrontation.

gloss_terse: Bocheru; personal name in Benjamin's genealogy
gloss_readable: A personal name appearing in Benjamite genealogies, specifically in the line of Saul. The name's form, ending in -û, reflects patterns found in other Hebrew names and possibly in Nabatean inscriptions. The name appears in the detailed genealogical records preserved in 1 Chronicles.

senses.1: Bocheru appears in parallel genealogies of Benjamin's descendants (1 Chronicles 8:38 = 9:44), specifically in the lineage connected to Saul's family. The name's form (בֹּכְרוּ) with its -û ending parallels other names like Gashmu and Melichu, suggesting a particular naming pattern. Scholars note possible connections to Nabatean name formations. Beyond his genealogical placement in Saul's extended family, no other information about this individual survives. The dual occurrence in Chronicles' parallel genealogies confirms the reading and importance of preserving even obscure family members in tribal records. Multilingual glosses simply transliterate (Bocru, Bochru), treating it as an opaque proper name whose etymology remains uncertain.
